category.faq.title: Questions this desk answers
category.llm.intro: The Language / LLM desk collects the repositories whose Hugging Face pipeline tag is text-generation: the chat and instruct models you load to answer a question, rewrite a paragraph or edit a repository. In the {days}-day window the desk picked up {count} repositories and {passed} of them pass the quality gate. Everything listed here publishes weights you can download, so the list is about files rather than hosted endpoints. A repository is filed by its pipeline tag first, then by tags and name patterns, and a precedence order settles the desk for a repo that looks like two things at once. Each row prints only the fields the source reports: parameter count, license, storage size, quantization, detected runners and an estimated VRAM figure. Those columns stay empty when Hugging Face does not publish the value, which is common, and an empty column is not a zero. The filters narrow by runner, parameter ceiling or license; the sort puts first-seen date, downloads or likes first; the model page carries the exact command for llama.cpp, Ollama, MLX or vLLM when the repository ships files those runners read. Two candidates side by side are on the compare page, and the glossary explains quantization, VRAM and the gate if a column is unfamiliar.
category.llm.faq.vram.q: How much VRAM does a local language model need?
category.llm.faq.vram.a: Weights take roughly the parameter count times the bytes per weight: about 0.5 GB per billion at 4-bit, 2 GB per billion at bf16. Add the KV cache, which the estimator puts at 0.15 GB per billion parameters for a 4096-token context and scales with the context you set. A 7B model at Q4_K_M is about 4 GB of weights before the KV cache.
category.llm.faq.run.q: How do I run one of these models locally?
category.llm.faq.run.a: Open a model page. When the repository ships files a known runner reads, the page prints the command: llama-cli -hf for GGUF weights, ollama run hf.co for a quantized repo, mlx_lm.generate on Apple silicon, vllm serve for a full-precision checkpoint. The repository id and the quantization come from the row itself, so the command matches the files you would download.
category.llm.faq.pick.q: Which language model should I pick?
category.llm.faq.pick.a: Start from the machine you have, not from a leaderboard. Filter the desk by parameter ceiling so the models left fit your memory, then sort by downloads to see what others load, check the license, and put two candidates on the compare page. The Radar does not score quality; it reports what Hugging Face publishes about each repository, and an empty spec means the value was never published. This window holds {count} repositories; {passed} of them pass the gate.
category.image.intro: The Image desk collects Hugging Face repositories tagged text-to-image, image-generation, image-to-image or image-editing: the diffusion families that turn a prompt, or an existing picture, into a new one. In the {days}-day window it picked up {count} repositories, {passed} of which pass the quality gate. Diffusion weights are large, so the precision a repository publishes is part of the decision: a full-precision checkpoint and a quantized single-file release are not the same download. The desk prints the storage size, the quantizations the file listing shows, the license and the parameter count when the repository reports them, and it estimates VRAM from the weights plus a KV cache the way it does on every other desk. Treat that estimate as a floor: image memory also grows with resolution, batch size and the number of sampling steps, and none of those live in the file listing. The runner column is more modest here than on the language desks. A diffusion checkpoint is usually loaded by the diffusers library or a diffusion front-end, so a one-line command appears only when the repository's own files map to a runner the Radar recognises. License deserves a look before a download: several image families ship non-commercial terms, and the filter can narrow the desk to a single license.
category.image.faq.vram.q: How much VRAM does an image model need?
category.image.faq.vram.a: The estimate on a row covers the weights at their published precision plus a KV cache for a chosen context. Image memory is larger than that figure because it also grows with output resolution, batch size and sampling steps, none of which is in the file listing. Treat the row as a starting point and leave headroom: a checkpoint that fits at 512 px can fail at 1024 px on the same card.
category.image.faq.run.q: How do I run a diffusion model locally?
category.image.faq.run.a: Diffusion checkpoints are usually loaded through the diffusers library or a diffusion front-end, so this desk rarely shows a one-line command. The page prints one only when the repository's files map to a runner the Radar detects, such as a GGUF file for llama.cpp or an MLX conversion. Otherwise it shows the weight format, the storage size and the repository link, which is what a front-end needs to load it.
category.image.faq.pick.q: Which image model should I choose?
category.image.faq.pick.a: Read the license first: several image families publish non-commercial terms, and the filter can narrow the desk to one license. Then compare storage size and quantization, because a smaller published precision is what makes a checkpoint run on a consumer card, and check which pipeline tags the repository carries. Downloads show what other people load, not what renders better; the Radar does not judge image quality. This window holds {count} repositories; {passed} of them pass the gate.
category.video.intro: The Video desk holds repositories tagged text-to-video, image-to-video, video-generation or video-to-video: models that produce a clip rather than a still. In the {days}-day window it collected {count} repositories and {passed} pass the quality gate. The figures on this page are the desk's own count for the window you selected, so they move when the window does. A video model is the most expensive kind of checkpoint on this site to run. The weight file tells you the parameter count and the precision when the repository reports them; the memory needed to decode a clip is a multiple of that, and it grows with frame count, resolution and steps. The VRAM figure on a row therefore covers weights and an estimated KV cache only - it is a floor, not a promise that a clip will render on a consumer card. Runners are the same story as on the image desk. Clip generation is normally driven by a library or a dedicated front-end rather than by llama.cpp or Ollama, so the one-line command prints only when the repository's files match a runner the Radar detects. Before you commit a download, read the license and the published precision; the filter row can narrow by license and by parameter ceiling, and the compare page puts two checkpoints next to each other.
category.video.faq.vram.q: How much VRAM does a video model need?
category.video.faq.vram.a: More than the row says. The estimate covers weights and an estimated KV cache, and video generation adds memory for every frame, for the resolution of the clip and for the sampling steps that produce it. A text-to-video checkpoint that fits at one short clip can fail at a longer one on the same card. Use the estimate as the floor and test with the clip length you actually need.
category.video.faq.run.q: Why is there no run command on some video models?
category.video.faq.run.a: Because the Radar only prints a command when the repository's files map to a runner it detects: llama.cpp, Ollama, MLX or vLLM. Video pipelines are usually driven by a library or a dedicated front-end, and a command invented for one would not work. The model page still shows the weight format, storage size and repository link, so you can wire it into the tool you already use.
category.video.faq.pick.q: Which video model should I pick?
category.video.faq.pick.a: Start from supported clip length and resolution, which the repository documents and the Radar does not measure, then look at the published precision and storage size to see whether the weights fit your machine. Filter by license before downloading. The desk is small, so sorting by downloads mostly shows which few checkpoints the community has adopted, not a quality ranking. This window holds {count} repositories; {passed} of them pass the gate.
category.coding.intro: The Coding desk is the one desk without a Hugging Face pipeline tag behind it. No tag on the Hub means "writes code", so the Radar files a repository here by name and tag patterns - code, coder, codex, coding, swe, agentic - and a precedence order puts coding above every other desk. A text-generation repository whose name or tags mark it as a coding model therefore lands here, not on the language desk. In the {days}-day window that rule collected {count} repositories, {passed} of which pass the gate. The desk mixes two kinds of release: base and instruct models tuned for code, and agent-oriented models built around tool calls and repository editing. Neither kind is measured by the Radar, so no row claims a benchmark score. What each row does carry is what Hugging Face reports - parameters, license, size, quantizations, detected runners - plus the VRAM estimate, which is the number that decides whether a 30B coder fits the machine you own. Filter by parameter ceiling before you sort by downloads: the most downloaded coding model in a window is often the largest one. The model page prints the exact command for llama.cpp, Ollama, MLX or vLLM when the files match, and the compare page puts two candidates on the same spec rows.
category.coding.faq.vram.q: How much VRAM does a coding model need?
category.coding.faq.vram.a: The same arithmetic as any language model: parameters times bytes per weight, plus a KV cache that grows with the context window. A 4-bit 7B coder is roughly 4 GB of weights; a 32B at the same precision is roughly 16 to 18 GB before the cache. That is why the parameter ceiling filter matters more here than on the small desks, and why the estimate is a floor.
category.coding.faq.run.q: How do I run a coding model locally?
category.coding.faq.run.a: Open the model page and copy the command. It is built from the repository id and the runner the files were detected with, so a GGUF repository gets llama-cli -hf or ollama run hf.co, an MLX conversion gets mlx_lm.generate, and a full-precision checkpoint gets vllm serve. Whether an editor or an agent framework can talk to it is a separate question the Radar does not answer.
category.coding.faq.pick.q: Which local coding model should I pick?
category.coding.faq.pick.a: Filter by parameter ceiling first, because a model that does not fit cannot help you, then sort by downloads to see what other people run, and check the license if the output goes into a product. Put two candidates on the compare page to see their specs on the same rows. Benchmark scores are self-reported, so the Radar prints none of them. This window holds {count} repositories; {passed} of them pass the gate.
category.audio.intro: The Audio desk gathers four different jobs under one key. It collects repositories tagged automatic-speech-recognition, audio-to-text, text-to-speech, music-generation and audio-classification: transcription, speech synthesis, music and sound classification. In the {days}-day window it picked up {count} repositories, {passed} of which pass the quality gate. Because the jobs differ, a single ranking would be meaningless. A transcription model returns text for a recording, a speech model returns a waveform for text, and a music model returns audio for a prompt; the row tells you which tags a repository carries, not which of those jobs you need. Filter by runner or license first, then read the model page before comparing sizes, because a speech model with few parameters is not a weaker model than a large one - it is a different task. The VRAM estimate prints when a repository reports a parameter count, and it covers weights plus a KV cache at a chosen context, not the memory a full audio pipeline allocates. The one-line command appears when the repository's files map to a runner the Radar knows, so check the model page rather than assuming.
category.audio.faq.vram.q: How much VRAM does an audio model need?
category.audio.faq.vram.a: The weights are small - a speech checkpoint is far smaller than the chat models on the language desk - and memory is often not the limiting factor. The estimate covers weights plus a KV cache at a chosen context and prints when the repository reports a parameter count. What a full audio pipeline allocates also depends on the length of the recording, the sample rate and the batch, so use the figure as a reference rather than a budget.
category.audio.faq.run.q: How do I run a speech model locally?
category.audio.faq.run.a: Check the model page: the Radar prints a one-line command only when the repository's files match a runner it detects, and many speech repositories are built for a task-specific library instead. The row still tells you the tags - transcription, speech synthesis, music, classification - and the weight format, which is what you need to choose between a GGUF conversion and the original checkpoint.
category.audio.faq.pick.q: Which audio model should I pick?
category.audio.faq.pick.a: Choose the task before the model. A transcription model returns text for a recording, a speech model returns audio for text, and the two are not substitutes; the row's pipeline tag says which one you are looking at. After that, sort by downloads for adoption, read the license, and check the language coverage the repository documents, which the Radar does not measure. This window holds {count} repositories; {passed} of them pass the gate.
category.multimodal.intro: The Multimodal desk collects repositories that answer questions about pictures and documents: Hugging Face pipeline tags visual-question-answering, image-to-text and document-question-answering, plus the multimodal, vlm and vision-language tags. The output is text about an image, which is what separates this desk from the image desk, where the output is a picture. In the {days}-day window the desk collected {count} repositories and {passed} pass the quality gate. Most of these are vision-language models: an image encoder bolted to a language model, so the memory a row quotes is the sum of both halves. The estimate is the same one used everywhere on the site - weights at the published precision plus a KV cache for a chosen context - and it says nothing about the resolution of the images you feed in, which is the other half of the cost. The desk is where readers look before they build a document pipeline or a screenshot reader. Sort by downloads to see what other people actually load, filter by parameter ceiling to keep a vision tower inside a laptop, and open the model page for the detected runners and the exact command when the files match one. The glossary covers context window and quantization, the two columns that decide whether a document fits in one pass.
category.multimodal.faq.vram.q: How much VRAM does a vision-language model need?
category.multimodal.faq.vram.a: More than a language model of the same parameter count, because the image encoder is part of the checkpoint. The estimate covers the published weights at their precision plus a KV cache, and it does not include the memory an image costs at the resolution you feed in. A model that fits at one image per request can fail on a batch, so leave headroom for the vision side.
category.multimodal.faq.run.q: How do I run a vision-language model locally?
category.multimodal.faq.run.a: The model page prints the command when the repository's files match a detected runner: a GGUF file gets llama-cli -hf or ollama run hf.co, an MLX conversion gets mlx_lm.generate, a full-precision checkpoint gets vllm serve. Not every vision-language repository publishes such files, and the page says so by showing the weight format and the repository link instead of a command.
category.multimodal.faq.pick.q: Which multimodal model should I pick?
category.multimodal.faq.pick.a: Start from the input you actually have: a photograph, a scanned document or a screenshot are different problems, and the pipeline tag on the row tells you which kind of repository this is. Then filter by parameter ceiling so the vision tower fits your card, check the license, and sort by downloads to see adoption. The Radar does not measure answer quality or OCR accuracy. This window holds {count} repositories; {passed} of them pass the gate.
category.embedding.intro: The Embedding desk collects models that turn text into vectors: Hugging Face pipeline tags feature-extraction and sentence-similarity, plus reranker tags. Nothing here writes an answer. These models score, retrieve and rank, and they are the part of a retrieval pipeline that decides what the language model gets to read. In the {days}-day window the desk picked up {count} repositories, {passed} of which pass the quality gate. Two jobs share the desk and they are not interchangeable. An embedder maps a passage to one vector so a search can compare it with a query; a reranker takes a query and a passage together and returns a score, which is slower and more accurate and is run on the top few candidates only. The row's tags say which is which, and the parameter column is the honest measure of cost, since these models are small and a run is bounded by how many passages you send through them. The VRAM estimate prints when a parameter count is reported, and for this desk the number that matters is usually the maximum sequence length the repository documents, not the footprint. Filter by license if the vectors feed a product, sort by downloads to see the current defaults, and read the model page for the weight format and the detected runners before wiring the model into a pipeline.
category.embedding.faq.vram.q: How much VRAM does an embedding model need?
category.embedding.faq.vram.a: These models are small: the weights are a fraction of what a chat model of the same parameter count costs elsewhere. The estimate prints when a count is reported and covers weights plus a KV cache at the context you choose. What actually bounds a retrieval run is how many passages you send through at once and how long they are, so watch the maximum sequence length more than the footprint.
category.embedding.faq.run.q: How do I serve an embedding model?
category.embedding.faq.run.a: Usually through a library or a serving stack rather than a chat runner, so the Radar prints a one-line command only when a repository's files map to a detected runner. The model page still lists the weight format, the storage size and the repository link, and the row names the pipeline tag: feature-extraction for an embedder, a sentence-similarity or reranker tag for the scoring half of a retrieval stack.
category.embedding.faq.pick.q: Which embedding model should I pick?
category.embedding.faq.pick.a: Decide whether you need an embedder or a reranker: an embedder maps a passage to one vector, a reranker scores a query and a passage together, and only the second can be run on a short candidate list. Then compare parameter count, the maximum sequence length the repository documents and the license. Downloads show which defaults other projects use, which is the closest thing to a ranking the desk has. This window holds {count} repositories; {passed} of them pass the gate.
category.vision.intro: The Vision desk holds the classic computer-vision tasks: object-detection, image-segmentation, depth-estimation, zero-shot-image-classification and image-classification. In each of them a picture goes in and labels, boxes, masks or a depth map come out; no text is generated, which is what keeps this desk apart from the multimodal one. In the {days}-day window it collected {count} repositories, {passed} of which pass the quality gate. Most of these checkpoints are far smaller than a language model, and the row prints the weight format the file listing shows. The row prints the storage size and the quantizations the file listing shows; the parameter count and the VRAM estimate appear when the repository reports them, and the estimate covers weights and a KV cache only. High-resolution input is the cost that does not show up in that figure. Runners are detected, not assumed. A repository whose files match llama.cpp, Ollama, MLX or vLLM gets a one-line command on its model page; a detection model exported for a vision runtime usually does not, and inventing one would be worse than leaving it out. Start from the task you need, filter by license and parameter ceiling, then compare two checkpoints on the same spec rows before you download.
category.vision.faq.vram.q: How much VRAM does a vision model need?
category.vision.faq.vram.a: Little for the weights, since most detection, segmentation and classification checkpoints are far smaller than a language model, and more for the input. The estimate covers weights plus a KV cache only, while memory grows with the resolution and the batch of images you feed in. If a run fails on a large image, lower the resolution before you change the model.
category.vision.faq.run.q: How do I run an object-detection or segmentation model?
category.vision.faq.run.a: Runners on this site are detected from file names and tags, and the four the Radar knows - llama.cpp, Ollama, MLX and vLLM - are built for language models, not for detectors. So the one-line command appears only when a repository's files happen to match one. Otherwise the model page gives you the weight format, the storage size and the repository link to load it in the runtime you use.
category.vision.faq.pick.q: Which vision model should I pick?
category.vision.faq.pick.a: Start from the task: detection, segmentation, depth, zero-shot classification and plain classification answer different questions, and the pipeline tag on the row says which one a repository is. Then check the license, the parameter count and the label set the repository documents, since a detector trained on the wrong classes will not help. Downloads show adoption inside the window, not accuracy. This window holds {count} repositories; {passed} of them pass the gate.
category.robotics.intro: The Robotics / Agent desk is the least uniform on the site. It collects repositories with the robotics pipeline tag, visual-document-retrieval repositories, and models tagged for function calling. A policy that drives a robot arm, a retriever that reads a document image and a language model that emits tool calls do not share a task, only a shelf. In the {days}-day window the desk picked up {count} repositories, {passed} of which pass the quality gate. Read the tags on a row before anything else. A function-calling model is a text model with a trained output format, so its parameter count and VRAM estimate behave like any language model. A robotics policy is a smaller network with a fixed input shape and an environment around it, and its weight file says very little about whether it will run on your hardware. That is why the runner column here often stays empty. The Radar prints a command only when a repository's files map to llama.cpp, Ollama, MLX or vLLM, and robot policies usually expect a simulation stack or a vendor SDK instead. Sort by downloads for the few models other people actually use, filter by license before you build on one, and treat this desk as a starting point that points back to the repository.
category.robotics.faq.vram.q: How much VRAM does a robotics or agent model need?
category.robotics.faq.vram.a: It depends on what you are looking at. A function-calling model is a language model, so the estimate behaves exactly as it does on the language desk: weights at the published precision plus a KV cache. A robotics policy is usually a smaller network with a fixed input shape, and the row's estimate covers its weights only; the environment it runs in is outside this site's measurement.
category.robotics.faq.run.q: How do I run a model from this desk?
category.robotics.faq.run.a: Check the model page for a command before assuming one exists. The Radar prints it only when the repository's files map to llama.cpp, Ollama, MLX or vLLM, and a robot policy generally expects a simulation stack or a vendor SDK instead. For function-calling models the command is the ordinary chat command for the detected runner.
category.robotics.faq.pick.q: Which robotics or agent model should I pick?
category.robotics.faq.pick.a: Read the repository before the row. This desk gathers three unrelated kinds of release, so the tags and the pipeline tag matter more than any shared ranking. For a function-calling model, filter by parameter ceiling and compare it like a language model. For a policy, check the license, the documented environment and the input shape, none of which the Radar measures. This window holds {count} repositories; {passed} of them pass the gate.
